beats.spoken_text: Why do you see the lightning before you hear the thunder?
By the end of this lesson you will be able to work it out.
Today we find out how fast a wave travels, and why.
Part 1: What a wave is.
A wave carries energy from one place to another.
The medium itself only moves back and forth around where it was.
Sound in air and light from the sun are both waves.
Drop a stone in a pond and ripples spread out.
The water stays where it is; the energy moves outwards.
Many people think a louder sound travels faster.
It does not: loudness changes the amplitude, and the speed stays the same.
Watch the pulse travel along the slinky while each coil stays put.
Part 2: Wave speed.
The wavelength is the distance between two neighbouring crests.
We write it with the Greek letter lambda and measure it in metres.
Frequency is how many waves pass a point each second.
The period is the time one wave takes to pass.
Amplitude is how far the medium moves from rest.
Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength.
Speed in metres per second, frequency in hertz, wavelength in metres.
Double the frequency at the same speed and the wavelength halves.
Before we go on: what happens to the wavelength if the frequency doubles?
Hold on to your guess. We will check it in a moment.
Let us try a note of four hundred and forty hertz in air.
We know the frequency and the speed of sound, three hundred and forty three.
Rearrange the equation so the wavelength is speed over frequency.
Divide, and the wavelength comes out at about seventy eight centimetres.
Sound moves at about three hundred and forty metres per second in air.
In water it is four times faster, and in steel faster still.
Here a wave moves along a string.
Each point only moves up and down.
Move the slider and watch the wavelength change with the frequency.
Here is the same calculation as a small Python function.
It takes the speed and the frequency and returns their ratio.
Running it prints about zero point seven eight metres.
Try this one. Pause the video if you need more time.
Six metres per second: two times three.
Without looking back: what does a wave carry?
And how do you find its speed?
Energy, not matter.
Speed is frequency times wavelength.
And the medium sets the speed.
A wave carries energy, not matter.
Its speed is frequency times wavelength.
And that speed depends on the medium.
Next time we use this to explain how we hear sound. See you then.
